USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Enter the early-October talks in Washington ready to convert China's goodwill gestures into a concrete purchase/partial-deal that freezes further escalation, while deliberately holding the existing tariff schedule (incl. the Oct 15-delayed hike) as leverage. Do not escalate further — the US economy is already showing strain from the trade war (inverted yield curve, contracting manufacturing, Fed rate cuts), and pushing harder risks tipping into recession and rattling markets with no enforcement gain. Do not concede unilaterally either; China has not yet put an offer on the table, so the correct posture is to negotiate toward an interim arrangement, not to pre-commit to a rollback.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading is moderate-high rather than existential. On one side, the dispute is materially biting the US real economy: the 10Y-2Y curve inverted in mid-August for the first time since 2007 (Washington Post 8/14), the ISM manufacturing index contracted in August for the first time since 2016 and the 10Y yield slid to a three-year low (CNBC 9/3), and the Fed has cut the fed funds rate from 2.40% in July to 2.04% (country_health FEDFUNDS) — a materially elevated recession risk that anchors near the +0.5 USA landmark. Consumer sentiment also fell to 89.8 in August before recovering to 93.2. On the other side, China is now offering concessions — exempting soybeans/pork from additional tariffs (Politico 9/13), publishing a 16-category tariff-exemption list (9/11), and making its first large US soybean purchases in months — and the US just delayed the next tariff hike to Oct 15 as a goodwill move, with talks scheduled for early October. Because the dispute's bite is real but receding and the US retains bargaining leverage, the threat sits at +0.45. The action stance is a mild positive (negotiate) because escalation at this fragile macro moment would deepen the economy's damage and hand markets a fresh scare, while a unilateral rollback would discard hard-won leverage before any formal Chinese offer exists. The disciplined move is to press, at the table, for a purchase-anchored interim deal and progress on enforcement — capturing China's concessions without committing to full settlement of the structurally hard issues.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Enter the imminent early-October talks from a posture of measured de-escalation — keep the goodwill gestures already made (16-category exemption, soybean/pork exemption, resumed farm purchases) but do not pre-commit to broad structural concessions before the US matches with a real tariff rollback. Continue negotiating toward a limited interim deal while holding firm on red lines (Huawei entity-list treatment, no surrender of Made in China 2025 autonomy).

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high for China, not existential. The dispute is already biting the real economy: official manufacturing PMI has been below 50 for four straight months (49.7 July, 49.5 August), industrial production growth fell to 4.8% in July (lowest since Feb 2002), PPI turned negative for the first time in three years, and US-bound exports fell 6.5% in July (timeline + SCMP/Forbes). By Sept 1, List 4A hit 15% (~$110–125B) and China's own $75B retaliation took effect, with a further $250B hike to 30% (Oct 15) and List 4B (Dec 15) still looming — meaning near-total tariff coverage on Chinese exports plus CNY breaking 7 and a US currency-manipulator designation. That justifies a clearly positive threat reading (~+0.5, 'major export sectors hit, FX pressure'). The action stance is de-escalatory rather than escalatory because China is under real economic strain (manufacturing contraction, weak external demand) and both sides are already signaling a truce: Trump delayed the Oct 1 hike to Oct 15 as a 'goodwill gesture,' and Beijing has matched with exemptions and resumed soybean buying (Reuters/Politico). Escalating further would risk the Oct 15 hike and deepen domestic pain (also amid swine-fever-driven food inflation and Hong Kong unrest); full concession would sacrifice red lines for no confirmed rollback. Hence hold the current posture and negotiate toward a limited deal (~+0.1).
